The American wigeon (Mareca americana) is a common dabbling duck of North American wetlands. Neonates emerge from eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] after a period of 23 days [ab = 23 days], which is typical for waterfowl of this body size. At hatching, downy young emerge with a wet weight at birth of approximately 24 grams [Wwb = approximately 24 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the precocial development strategy of Anatidae. These chicks are capable of leaving the nest shortly after hatching and begin foraging independently under the watchful supervision of the attending female. The initial wet weight recorded immediately after emergence from the egg is approximately 42.7 grams [Ww0 = approximately 42.7 grams], representing the mass of the freshly hatched chick after the absorption of residual yolk and the drying of natal down. This value is slightly higher than the mass measured shortly thereafter, as the chick loses some residual moisture in the first hours of life.

Field studies have documented that fledging, the point at which flight feathers are sufficiently developed for sustained flight, occurs approximately 40 days after hatching [tx = approximately 40 days after hatching]. However, this milestone shows considerable variation within the species, with published accounts indicating a range of 37 to 48 days. The timing of fledging is influenced by factors such as local food availability, brood size, and the body condition of the attending female. The age at puberty, marking the onset of reproductive capability, is reached at approximately 120 days after hatching [tp = approximately 120 days after hatching], though most individuals do not breed until their second calendar year. This delay reflects the time required for young birds to complete their first prebasic molt, acquire adult plumage, and establish sufficient body condition to support the energetic demands of reproduction. The relatively rapid progression from hatching to physiological maturity is characteristic of many northern-breeding dabbling ducks.

The maximum lifespan recorded for American wigeon in the wild is approximately 21.3 years [am = approximately 21.3 years], a figure derived from long-term banding studies across the species' breeding range in the boreal forests of Canada and Alaska. This longevity is notable for a relatively small-bodied dabbler and suggests a life-history strategy built around low annual adult mortality rather than high fecundity. Adult body mass shows pronounced sexual size dimorphism, consistent with patterns observed in many dabbling ducks. The ultimate wet weight for females, representing the asymptotic adult mass, is approximately 710 grams [Wwi = approximately 710 grams], whereas males attain a substantially larger average adult mass of 792 grams [Wwi = 792 grams]. This difference in body mass likely reflects divergent selective pressures: males benefit from larger body size during aggressive courtship displays and territory defense, while females remain at a smaller size that may confer energetic advantages during the demanding incubation period.

Reproductive output in American wigeon follows a pattern typical of many northern-hemisphere ducks. Females lay a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with a mean clutch size of approximately 9 eggs per nest [N_R_i = approximately 9 eggs per nest]. This combination of moderate clutch size and single annual nesting effort yields a maximum annual reproductive rate that is comparatively modest for a dabbling duck. The time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days], meaning that females hatching early in one breeding season are physiologically capable of nesting the following spring at approximately one year of age. In practice, a substantial proportion of first-year females defer breeding or experience nest failure due to inexperience or poor body condition, so effective recruitment into the breeding population often occurs at a slightly older age. Nest success is heavily influenced by predation pressure from mesocarnivores such as raccoons and striped skunks.

American wigeon are primarily herbivorous dabbling ducks, foraging extensively on aquatic vegetation, including pondweeds, sedges, and the leaves of submerged macrophytes. Their distinctive short, stout bill is well-adapted for grazing on tender shoots and for pulling up plant matter from shallow water. During the non-breeding season, large flocks form in coastal estuaries and inland lakes across the southern United States, Mexico, and Central America. They are known for their commensal feeding behavior, often grazing in close association with American coots and other waterfowl to exploit disturbed vegetation. The maximum reproduction rate for the species is 9 eggs per year [Ri = 9 eggs per year], a value that aligns closely with predictions based on body size and dietary ecology. This moderate reproductive investment is balanced by relatively high adult survival, as suggested by the species' maximum lifespan. The species' ecological flexibility and broad geographic distribution make it a valuable subject for comparative life-history studies within the Anatini.
